records.name: AugmentedDescartes.lorentz_sphereRow_self
records.entry_name: The augmented Descartes theorem in every dimension, its converses, and Soddy's two spheres
records.doc: A Lean 4 development of Section 3 of Lagarias, Mallows and Wilks, Beyond the Descartes circle theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 109 (2002) 338-361), in the Lorentz form. An oriented sphere in R^n with centre x and signed radius r has the augmented curvature-centre row (|x|^2/r - r, 1/r, x/r); an oriented hyperplane <h, y> = delta with unit normal h has the row (2 delta, 0, h) (LMW Definition 3.2, (3.7)-(3.9)). Tangency is distance-encoded in LMW's oriented sense: two spheres dist^2 = (r + s)^2 (external tangency for two positive radii, internal when one radius is negative), a sphere and a hyperplane <h, x> - delta = -r, two hyperplanes opposite unit normals, LMW's oriented tangency pair by pair, and the converses deliver tangency in this sense; the compatible orientations of an oriented Descartes configuration (disjoint interiors, with the given orientations or all reversed) are proved separately for every solution, after multiplying each row's power polynomial by the total curvature, and for a valid, pairwise tangent family with positive total curvature for its own open interiors. Kernel-checked, for every n >= 1 (LMW's Section 3 assumes n >= 2; their Section 8, (8.4), is the identity on the line): the augmented matrix W of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres of nonzero curvature, and of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres and hyperplanes, satisfies W^T Q_n W = [[0, -4, 0], [-4, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2 I_n]] with Q_n = I - (1/n) 11^T (Theorem 3.3); every real solution W is the augmented matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes, and, when its second column has no zero, of exactly one pairwise tangent family of spheres (the converse of Theorem 3.3); the Soddy-Gosset relation (sum 1/r_i)^2 = n sum (1/r_i)^2 with and without hyperplanes (Theorem 1.2, (1.2)) and its form b^T Q_n b = 0 ((3.2)); the curvature-centre identity M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) (Theorem 3.2, (3.5)); at n = 2 the complex Descartes theorem (sum b_i z_i)^2 = 2 sum (b_i z_i)^2 and sum b_i (b_i z_i) = (1/2)(sum b_i)(sum b_i z_i) (Theorem 2.1, (2.2)-(2.3)); det Q_n = -2/n; and the three statements for Mathlib's EuclideanGeometry.Sphere (pairwise IsExtTangent, or one enclosing sphere to which the others are IsIntTangent, with curvature -1/r_e). The matrix identity is proved as LMW's Section 4 argument (Lemmas 4.3-4.4, (4.9)-(4.10)) run directly in Euclidean coordinates: W^T Q_n W is the target exactly when the rows of W have Lorentz norm 1 and pair to -1 under G = [[0, -1/2, 0], [-1/2, 0, 0], [0, 0, I_n]], since W G W^T = 2I - J and (2I - J)(Q_n/2) = I. Also proved: both halves of the converse of the Soddy-Gosset theorem, LMW's Theorem 3.1, about which they write "We do not know an easy proof of this result; a proof appears in [16]" ([16] is Graham-Lagarias-Mallows-Wilks-Yan III, whose arXiv versions 1-2 prove both halves as their Theorem 2.2 from the same base configuration and the transitivity of the Lorentz group, a section the published version omits). Existence: every nonzero b with (sum b_i)^2 = n sum b_i^2 is the curvature vector of a pairwise tangent family of spheres, where b_i is nonzero, and hyperplanes, where b_i = 0, and of a family of spheres when no b_i vanishes, by one Q_n-reflection from the configuration of two parallel hyperplanes and n unit spheres in the proof of GLMWY III's Theorem 6.1, or from its inversion in the unit sphere. Congruence: two valid, pairwise tangent families with the same curvatures, index by index, are carried one to the other by exactly one Euclidean motion x -> x O + t with O^T O = I, reflections and hyperplanes included, with O = (1/2) X^T Q_n X' and t = -(1/4) a^T Q_n X' for augmented matrices [a | b | X] and [a' | b | X'] and the motion's action on points, spheres and hyperplanes; W_1^-1 W_2 preserves the target form and fixes the curvature coordinate, and every such matrix is a motion matrix (GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 argue instead by the rigidity of a simplex of centres); its uniqueness and parameters are proved here. A motion preserves validity, curvature and tangency, so two valid, pairwise tangent families are congruent exactly when their curvature vectors agree. For every solution W: the total curvature B is nonzero, the open sets {y : B F_i(y) < 0}, F_i(y) = b_i |y|^2 - 2 <v_i, y> + a_i the power polynomial of row i (negative exactly inside a ball, outside a ball of negative radius, or on the side of a hyperplane its normal points to), are pairwise disjoint, at most two rows are hyperplanes, and no three boundaries pass through a finite point; for a valid, pairwise tangent family the total curvature is nonzero, at most two members are hyperplanes, and when the total curvature is positive the open interiors are pairwise disjoint. The converse of Theorem 3.2 in every dimension under the hypothesis of a nonzero first column (every real M with M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) and a nonzero first column is the curvature-centre matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes), which GLMWY I, Theorem 3.1 and its Remark, prove at n = 2 with that hypothesis and which LMW's printed converse ("any real solution M") and GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 Theorem 2.3 omit, together with the matrix at n = 2 with columns 0, e_0 - e_1, e_2 - e_3 (GLMWY I's configuration (3.15) with its first column zeroed; the matrix of four oriented lines with normals +-e_0, +-e_1), which solves the equation and is the curvature-centre matrix of no valid, pairwise tangent family. The existence of a configuration in every dimension (that configuration); for n >= 2 the Apollonian generators S_k = I + (2/(n-1)) e_k 1^T - (2n/(n-1)) e_k e_k^T of GLMWY III, (4.1), preserve Q_n and carry configurations to configurations, with the row formula (S_k W)_k = (2/(n-1)) sum_{i != k} W_i - W_k, and Soddy's two spheres (LMW, footnote 3; GLMWY III, Section 4.1), in the signed sense: the oriented spheres and hyperplanes tangent to n + 1 members of a configuration are exactly the missing member and its Apollonian reflection, two distinct objects whose curvatures sum to (2/(n-1)) times the sum of the others' curvatures. The planar Soddy-Gosset relation for four circles of positive radius, pairwise externally tangent or with one enclosing circle, is already in Lean in facebookresearch/atlas-lean (descartes_circle_theorem, not registered); rjwalters/lean-genius and carlok/LeanFrontier treat the planar relation as a definition (its two roots, the same over the complex numbers, integer reflections and parity; LeanFrontier checks it for one family of Ford circles and their tangent line), with no derivation from tangency; no other formalization of these statements was found by the dated searches.

Kernel-checked, for every n >= 1 (LMW's Section 3 assumes n >= 2; their Section 8, (8.4), is the identity on the line): the augmented matrix W of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres of nonzero curvature, and of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres and hyperplanes, satisfies W^T Q_n W = [[0, -4, 0], [-4, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2 I_n]] with Q_n = I - (1/n) 11^T (Theorem 3.3); every real solution W is the augmented matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes, and, when its second column has no zero, of exactly one pairwise tangent family of spheres (the converse of Theorem 3.3); the Soddy-Gosset relation (sum 1/r_i)^2 = n sum (1/r_i)^2 with and without hyperplanes (Theorem 1.2, (1.2)) and its form b^T Q_n b = 0 ((3.2)); the curvature-centre identity M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) (Theorem 3.2, (3.5)); at n = 2 the complex Descartes theorem (sum b_i z_i)^2 = 2 sum (b_i z_i)^2 and sum b_i (b_i z_i) = (1/2)(sum b_i)(sum b_i z_i) (Theorem 2.1, (2.2)-(2.3)); det Q_n = -2/n; and the three statements for Mathlib's EuclideanGeometry.Sphere (pairwise IsExtTangent, or one enclosing sphere to which the others are IsIntTangent, with curvature -1/r_e). The matrix identity is proved as LMW's Section 4 argument (Lemmas 4.3-4.4, (4.9)-(4.10)) run directly in Euclidean coordinates: W^T Q_n W is the target exactly when the rows of W have Lorentz norm 1 and pair to -1 under G = [[0, -1/2, 0], [-1/2, 0, 0], [0, 0, I_n]], since W G W^T = 2I - J and (2I - J)(Q_n/2) = I. Also proved: both halves of the converse of the Soddy-Gosset theorem, LMW's Theorem 3.1, about which they write "We do not know an easy proof of this result; a proof appears in [16]" ([16] is Graham-Lagarias-Mallows-Wilks-Yan III, whose arXiv versions 1-2 prove both halves as their Theorem 2.2 from the same base configuration and the transitivity of the Lorentz group, a section the published version omits). Existence: every nonzero b with (sum b_i)^2 = n sum b_i^2 is the curvature vector of a pairwise tangent family of spheres, where b_i is nonzero, and hyperplanes, where b_i = 0, and of a family of spheres when no b_i vanishes, by one Q_n-reflection from the configuration of two parallel hyperplanes and n unit spheres in the proof of GLMWY III's Theorem 6.1, or from its inversion in the unit sphere. Congruence: two valid, pairwise tangent families with the same curvatures, index by index, are carried one to the other by exactly one Euclidean motion x -> x O + t with O^T O = I, reflections and hyperplanes included, with O = (1/2) X^T Q_n X' and t = -(1/4) a^T Q_n X' for augmented matrices [a | b | X] and [a' | b | X'] and the motion's action on points, spheres and hyperplanes; W_1^-1 W_2 preserves the target form and fixes the curvature coordinate, and every such matrix is a motion matrix (GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 argue instead by the rigidity of a simplex of centres); its uniqueness and parameters are proved here. A motion preserves validity, curvature and tangency, so two valid, pairwise tangent families are congruent exactly when their curvature vectors agree. For every solution W: the total curvature B is nonzero, the open sets {y : B F_i(y) < 0}, F_i(y) = b_i |y|^2 - 2 <v_i, y> + a_i the power polynomial of row i (negative exactly inside a ball, outside a ball of negative radius, or on the side of a hyperplane its normal points to), are pairwise disjoint, at most two rows are hyperplanes, and no three boundaries pass through a finite point; for a valid, pairwise tangent family the total curvature is nonzero, at most two members are hyperplanes, and when the total curvature is positive the open interiors are pairwise disjoint. The converse of Theorem 3.2 in every dimension under the hypothesis of a nonzero first column (every real M with M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) and a nonzero first column is the curvature-centre matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes), which GLMWY I, Theorem 3.1 and its Remark, prove at n = 2 with that hypothesis and which LMW's printed converse ("any real solution M") and GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 Theorem 2.3 omit, together with the matrix at n = 2 with columns 0, e_0 - e_1, e_2 - e_3 (GLMWY I's configuration (3.15) with its first column zeroed; the matrix of four oriented lines with normals +-e_0, +-e_1), which solves the equation and is the curvature-centre matrix of no valid, pairwise tangent family. The existence of a configuration in every dimension (that configuration); for n >= 2 the Apollonian generators S_k = I + (2/(n-1)) e_k 1^T - (2n/(n-1)) e_k e_k^T of GLMWY III, (4.1), preserve Q_n and carry configurations to configurations, with the row formula (S_k W)_k = (2/(n-1)) sum_{i != k} W_i - W_k, and Soddy's two spheres (LMW, footnote 3; GLMWY III, Section 4.1), in the signed sense: the oriented spheres and hyperplanes tangent to n + 1 members of a configuration are exactly the missing member and its Apollonian reflection, two distinct objects whose curvatures sum to (2/(n-1)) times the sum of the others' curvatures. The planar Soddy-Gosset relation for four circles of positive radius, pairwise externally tangent or with one enclosing circle, is already in Lean in facebookresearch/atlas-lean (descartes_circle_theorem, not registered); rjwalters/lean-genius and carlok/LeanFrontier treat the planar relation as a definition (its two roots, the same over the complex numbers, integer reflections and parity; LeanFrontier checks it for one family of Ford circles and their tangent line), with no derivation from tangency; no other formalization of these statements was found by the dated searches.

records.name: AlexandroffUrysohn.IsMetrizingSequence.exists_uniformity
records.entry_name: Alexandroff–Urysohn cover metrization
records.doc: A T0 space is metrizable if and only if it admits a sequence of open covers such that every intersecting pair of members at the next level has union contained in one member at the current level, and the point-stars form a neighborhood basis. Without separation the same criterion characterizes pseudometrizability. The proof constructs a countably generated co-membership uniformity with exactly the supplied topology. Covers have unrestricted cardinality; empty spaces are included. Classical mathematics, with no novelty or priority claim.

records.name: Palomar656.erdos_656
records.entry_name: Erdős Problem 656: translated restricted pair sums
records.doc: A reproduction of a complete Lean proof that every set A of natural numbers with positive ordinary upper asymptotic density contains an infinite subset B whose distinct pair sums, after one integer translation, all lie in A. This is the exact ordinary-density statement of Erdős Problem 656, an instance of Kra–Moreira–Richter–Robertson Theorem 1.2(i).

records.name: Waists.sphere_waist
records.entry_name: Waist
records.doc: Formalization of waist inequalities for different settings: (1) Gromov's waist theorem for the round sphere S^n (the original proof in Memarian arXiv:0911.3972 has gaps; here a spherical adaptation of Klartag's proof is used); (2) An explicit positive lower bound on the unnormalized (n-k)-dimensional Hausdorff measure (Mathlib's muH[n-k], defined via sum of (diam U_i)^{n-k} without the unit-ball normalization factor omega_{n-k} / 2^{n-k}, in the chordal metric on S^n) of a fiber on the round sphere S^n: muH[n-k](f^{-1}(y)) >= 1 / (12 * 4^n * 3^k), yielding the positive lower bound (omega_{n-k} / 2^{n-k}) / (12 * 4^n * 3^k) for conventionally normalized Hausdorff measure (motivated by Gromov's 2003 conjecture of the sharp bound vol(S^{n-k}), which remains open for 1 < k < n; proved via Akopyan modification of Klartag's argument, Waists.sphere_hausdorff_waist); (3) The Gaussian waist inequality on (R^n, gamma_n) (Gromov 2003, Klartag arXiv:1608.04121); (4) The waist of the open unit cube (0,1)^n (Klartag arXiv:1608.04121); (5) The waist of the Euclidean ball B^n(R) with arbitrary center and radius (Akopyan-Karasev, arXiv:1608.06279); (6) The waist of a spherical ball of radius R < pi in S^n (Akopyan-Karasev, arXiv:1702.07513); (7) The waist of a hyperbolic ball of radius R in H^n (Akopyan-Karasev, arXiv:1702.07513); (8) The waist of an ellipsoid with semi-axes a_1 <= ... <= a_n (Akopyan-Karasev, arXiv:1608.06279, Corollary 1); (9) The waist of a box / parallelotope (0, a_1) x ... x (0, a_n) (Akopyan-Karasev, arXiv:1608.06279, Corollary 2). Supporting developments include: classical and tree Borsuk-Ulam theorems derived from combinatorial Tucker-type lemmas; Prékopa-Leindler and Brunn-Minkowski inequalities; spherical cap quasiconcavity; Archimedes' projection; and Frostman center measures.

records.entry_name: Füredi's stability theorem and the Erdős–Simonovits stability theorem
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the stability theory of Turán's theorem. (1) Füredi's sharp stability theorem for cliques: a K_{p+1}-free graph on n vertices with at least t(n, p) − t edges (t(n, p) the number of edges of the Turán graph) has a p-partite subgraph with at least e(G) − t edges, via Füredi's partition inequality e(G) + Σᵢ e(G[Vᵢ]) ≤ e(K(V₁, …, V_p)); also edit distance at most 3t to a complete p-partite graph. (2) The Erdős–Simonovits stability theorem for every forbidden graph L with χ(L) ≤ p + 1: for every ε > 0 there are δ > 0 and n₀ such that every L-free graph on n ≥ n₀ vertices with at least (1 − 1/p) n²/2 − δn² edges differs from a complete p-partite graph in at most εn² edges, derived as in Füredi's paper from the regularity method. For this, the project extends Mathlib's regularity theory, which only treats triangles, with (3) the clique counting lemma in ε-uniform parts, (4) the clique removal lemma (fewer than δn^r copies of K_r can be destroyed by deleting fewer than εn² edges) and (5) the embedding lemma for any fixed graph with a proper colouring into pairwise uniform dense parts. Mathlib has Turán's theorem, Szemerédi's regularity lemma and triangle counting/removal, but none of (1)–(5).

records.name: Gluck.Discrete.tabachnikov_converse_geometric
records.entry_name: A converse to the discrete four-vertex theorem
records.doc: Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the paper "A converse to the discrete four-vertex theorem", answering Tabachnikov's Problem 2. For every n >= 4, every cyclic sequence of positive numbers with two distinct plateau maxima and two distinct plateau minima is the sequence of circumradii of consecutive vertex triples of a simple, strictly convex, coherent polygon (circumcenters inside the vertex angles). Together with Dahlberg's discrete four-vertex theorem, also proved here, this characterizes the nonconstant radius sequences of such polygons. The realization can be chosen C^1 in the data near every nonconstant admissible sequence, but an explicit path of hexagon data admits no continuous choice of realizing polygons. The analogous characterization for circles tangent to three consecutive supporting lines (the converse to Wegner's four-edge theorem) is also proved.

records.name: Erdos662.not_globalThresholdConjecture
records.entry_name: Erdos 662: corrected global threshold conjecture
records.doc: Disproves an explicitly corrected global threshold formulation of Erdos problem 662. For each radius, the conjecture bounds the average number of nearby points in every sufficiently large one-separated planar set by the unit triangular lattice's neighbor count. An exact rational oblique lattice and separated finite replicas violate the bound at radius six.

records.name: Sneider.exists_closed_countable_nhds_basis_of_isGδ
records.entry_name: Sneider's Gδ-diagonal metrization theorem
records.doc: A compact Hausdorff space is metrizable if and only if its diagonal is a Gδ subset of its square with the product topology. The proof supplies a cofinal countable family of finite intersections of closed diagonal neighborhoods and an actual metric inducing exactly the given topology. The underlying type is arbitrary and may be empty. A general supporting theorem proves countable neighborhood character of every closed Gδ set in a compact normal space. This is classical mathematics; no novelty or priority is claimed.

records.name: PseudorandomMatchings.theorem_1_1
records.entry_name: Pseudorandom hypergraph matchings (Ehard–Glock–Joos)
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the main results of Ehard, Glock and Joos, "Pseudorandom hypergraph matchings" (Combin. Probab. Comput. 2020): Pippenger's theorem on almost perfect matchings in almost regular hypergraphs with small codegrees (Theorem 1.1); the existence of a matching M in any r-uniform hypergraph with Δ(H) ≤ Δ, codegrees ≤ Δ^{1−δ} and at most exp(Δ^{ε²}) edges such that ω(M) = (1 ± Δ^{−ε}) ω(E(H))/Δ simultaneously for up to exp(Δ^{ε²}) weight functions (Theorem 1.2, with ε = δ/(50r²)); the generalization to weight functions on ℓ-tuples of edges, under the same exponential cap on the number of edges and of weight functions (Theorem 1.3, the main theorem, with ε = δ/(50L²r²)); the concentration inequality for pattern weights under a uniformly random colouring (Theorem 3.1); and the existence of partial Steiner systems whose subgraph counts behave as in the random model (Theorem 4.1). The formal proof is self-contained over Mathlib: Freedman's and Bernstein's inequalities are proved inside the project, and the Molloy–Reed colouring theorem used as a black box in the paper is replaced by a self-contained nibble.

records.name: KKP117.strengthened_asymptotic
records.entry_name: A sharp asymptotic spectral bound for forbidden subgraphs
records.doc: For every fixed finite graph F of chromatic number r+1 at least three and every positive epsilon, there is an edge threshold M such that every finite simple F-free graph G with m at least M satisfies F2(A_G) <= 2(1-1/r)m - (2(1-1/r)-1)Delta(G) + epsilon m. F2 is the sum of the squares of the two largest positive adjacency eigenvalues with missing terms padded by zero. The graphs may be disconnected. A companion theorem establishes agreement with the two largest ordered eigenvalue squares in the same eventual range. Enough edges force an F-free graph to be noncomplete; BN nonedge interlacing gives a nonnegative second ordered eigenvalue, so its positive-two energy equals the first two ordered eigenvalue squares. The proof checks ordinary clique removal through regularity and clique counting, derives weighted deletion, reuses the proved BN rank-two Gram inequality, and supplies the spectral lift, hub separation and uniform assembly.

records.name: RRExact.real_counterexample
records.entry_name: Low-dimensional exact counterexamples to the Recht–Ré inequality
records.doc: Five real symmetric PSD 3×3 integer matrices and five complex Hermitian PSD 2×2 Gaussian-integer matrices each have sum 100I and exact norm-of-averaged-product ratio 10329/10000 at n=k=5. The Lean statements use Mathlib positive semidefiniteness over the real and complex fields and the Euclidean operator norm. The rational formalization of De Sa's dimension-five norm-19/16 example is included as a supporting benchmark. The real symmetric dimension-two case is not resolved.

records.name: QuarticLyapunov.endpoint_classification
records.entry_name: Sharp quartic Lyapunov boundaries and sextic separation for a planar cubic family
records.doc: For a specified planar homogeneous cubic family, positive definite real homogeneous quartic Lyapunov certificates exist with strict derivative exactly when the absolute parameter is below an explicit algebraic boundary, and with weak derivative exactly through that boundary. Its value is about 2.1281535330886186. At the positive endpoint the entire cone of quartics with nonpositive derivative is one explicit nonnegative ray, without any positivity assumption. The negative Lie derivative of the endpoint quartic is a cubic square with three distinct real zero lines. Exact integer certificates separate degrees two and four at parameter two, and degrees four and six at nine fourths. The formal statements use actual partial derivatives and allow unrestricted real coefficients.

records.name: NashWilliamsTutte.tree_packing
records.entry_name: The Nash-Williams–Tutte tree packing theorem and Nash-Williams' arboricity theorem
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of three classical results on edge-disjoint trees and forests in finite simple graphs, none of which is in Mathlib. (1) The Nash-Williams–Tutte tree packing theorem: a graph has k edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if every partition of its vertices into m parts has at least k(m − 1) edges between different parts. (2) Nash-Williams' arboricity theorem: the edges can be covered by k forests if and only if every nonempty vertex set S spans at most k(|S| − 1) edges. (3) The corollary that every 2k-edge-connected graph has k edge-disjoint spanning trees. Mathlib has no matroid union theorem and no graphic matroid; the proofs are direct edge-exchange arguments.

records.name: ErdosGirthChromatic.exists_girth_indep
records.entry_name: Erdős' theorem on graphs of large girth and large chromatic number
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Erdős' 1959 theorem: for every g and k there is a finite graph with girth greater than g and chromatic number greater than k. The formalization proves the structural form given by Erdős' probabilistic argument: for every g and every ε > 0, for all sufficiently large n there is a graph on n vertices with no cycle of length at most g in which every independent set has fewer than εn vertices; hence, for all large n, a graph on n vertices with girth greater than g that is not k-colourable. Mathlib has girth and chromatic number but not this theorem; Mycielski's construction (registered separately by another author) gives triangle-free graphs only.

records.name: RenyiMonotonicity.renyi_monotone
records.entry_name: Rényi and Tsallis entropy monotonicity for Bernoulli sums
records.doc: Lean formalization of coordinatewise Rényi and Tsallis entropy monotonicity for finite independent Bernoulli sums on the closed half cube, for every real order in [0,2], as stated in Hillion-Johnson Conjecture 4.4. The complete core proves both entropy comparisons and the finite inverse-score association inequality. Concrete coefficient-law and entropy definitions are checked separately. VERIFICATION.md defines exact-source Linux acceptance and distinguishes historical association-only checkpoints.

records.name: CountableNetwork.IsNetwork.exists_bounded_separating_family
records.entry_name: Compact Hausdorff countable-network metrization
records.doc: For an arbitrary compact Hausdorff space, metrizability and second countability are each equivalent to the existence of a countable network of arbitrary subsets. A genuine Urysohn-function construction from pairs of network elements supplies continuous separation, and a compatible metric induces exactly the original topology. Supporting results give bounded-real-coordinate closed embeddings, preservation under continuous surjections, arbitrary-subspace heredity and compact-subspace metrization. Empty spaces and arbitrary universes are allowed. This is classical mathematics; no novelty or priority is claimed.

records.name: SizeRamsey.four_mul_tau4_le_edgeCount
records.entry_name: The connected size-Ramsey number of a four-edge matching versus a quadrilateral
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization project for the connected size-Ramsey equality rhat_c(4K2, C4) = 17. The intended proof uses a universal C4 vertex-transversal bound 4 tau_4(G) <= |E(G)|, a classification of the connected equality cases through sixteen edges (C4, the 4-wheel, K_{3,3} minus an edge, the octahedron), an avoiding-colouring construction from a three-vertex transversal, and an explicit twelve-vertex, seventeen-edge host. Proofs are complete as of commit c8d54e2 (2026-10-17); the proof certificate is Solution.lean and its dependency closure. Formal adversary pass 1 and reviewer pass 1 are ACCEPT_WITH_FIXES (fixes applied); the CI comparator passed at 38bd345 (2026-10-17) with five records. A sixth record, the transversal half of Corollary C (SizeRamsey.connected_transversal_le_three), was registered on 2026-10-17 (commit cc2aec2); the CI comparator passed with six records at 46bf2d0 (2026-10-17, run 39034260971).

records.name: TriangleGrowth.growth_series
records.entry_name: Growth series of the triangle Coxeter groups (p, q, infinity), with the PGL(2,Z) instance: Padovan sphere sizes and growth rate the plastic number
records.doc: Kernel-checked proof, for every Coxeter system on three generators a, b, c with m(a,c) = p, m(b,c) = q, m(a,b) = infinity and p, q >= 2, of the growth-series identity in the ring of integer power series: (sum_n a(n) X^n) * (1 - (X + ... + X^(p-1))(X + ... + X^(q-1))) = (1 + X)(1 + ... + X^(p-1))(1 + ... + X^(q-1)), where a(n) is the number of group elements of Coxeter length n; together with its instances (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf), (3,3,inf) and, for (2,3,inf) = PGL(2,Z), the sphere sizes 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 16, ..., the Padovan identity a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, the two-sided bounds 2 rho^n <= a(n) <= 4 rho^n (n >= 2), and the growth rate a(n)^(1/n) -> rho, the plastic number, the unique real root > 1 of x^3 = x + 1; and, for the whole family, monotonicity and symmetry in (p, q), the growth rate of every hyperbolic member, and the minimality of the plastic number. Twenty compared theorems: (1) the general identity for all p, q >= 2; (2) non-vacuity, a Coxeter matrix of that type exists for all p, q >= 2; (3)-(5) the three instances; (6) the (2,3,inf) sphere sizes a(0..4) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and the recursion a(n+5) = a(n+3) + a(n+2) for all n; (7) that the recursion fails one step earlier, a(4) != a(2) + a(1); (8) a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, for any sequence with the Padovan initial values and recursion; (9) existence and uniqueness of the plastic number; (10) the bounds; (11) the n-th-root limit; (12) monotonicity: a(n) of a (p,q,inf) system is at most a(n) of a (p',q',inf) system for p <= p', q <= q'; (13) symmetry in p and q; (14) 2 rho^n <= a(n), n >= 2, for every hyperbolic member; (15) for (p,q) != (2,2) exactly one tau > 1 solves (tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(p-1))(tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(q-1)) = 1; (16) a(n)^(1/n) -> tau; (17) tau strictly increasing in (p,q); (18) rho <= tau with equality exactly at (2,3), (3,2), so the plastic number is the minimal growth rate of the family; (19) tau < 2; (20) tau -> 2 as p, q -> infinity (for every sigma < 2 there is N with tau > sigma whenever p, q >= N). The family statements (12)-(20) give the growth rate of every hyperbolic (p, q, inf) group as the unique root tau > 1 of an explicit equation, strictly increasing in the labels, with the plastic number as the family minimum attained only at (2,3,inf) and (3,2,inf); they restrict to this family, and kernel-check there, Terragni's monotonicity (2016, Thm. A), Floyd's planar minimality (1992, p. 482) and the continuity of the growth rate (Floyd 1992; Yukita 2024). The mathematics is classical and no novelty is claimed for it: the growth series of a Coxeter group is rational and determined by its finite parabolic subgroups (Steinberg 1968; Humphreys 1990 Section 5.12); growth of planar hyperbolic Coxeter groups is Floyd 1992 and Cannon-Wagreich 1992, and the (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf) and (3,3,inf) sphere sequences are OEIS A096231, A179070 (shifted) and A054886, with generating functions derived there from Cannon-Wagreich Prop. 3.1 and, for A096231, the Padovan form a(n) = A000931(n+10) recorded; Floyd 1992 (p. 482) proves (2,3,inf) minimal among cusped planar groups and Kellerhals 2013 gives an alternative proof; Bucher-Talambutsa 2016 Prop. 18 proves statement (11) itself by a normal form and, with Mann's bound, the minimality of rho for PGL(2,Z) over all generating sets. The (p, q, inf) family is hyperbolic exactly when (p, q) differs from (2, 2); the affine (2, 2, inf) is included in (1). The contribution claimed is the kernel-checked general identity for all p, q at once, and the family statements (12)-(20) derived from it, from Mathlib's CoxeterSystem alone — Mathlib at this pin has no growth series, no exchange or deletion property and no parabolic-subgroup API — by constructing the amalgam normal forms, lifting their action to the group, proving Coxeter length equals normal-form length, and counting. No "first formalization" claim is made. Application, cited and not a claim of the entry: the (2,3,inf) group is the Weyl group of AE_3 = PGL(2,Z) (Feingold-Frenkel 1983) and, in the Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai billiard description of the Belinski-Khalatnikov-Lifshitz limit (a conjecture for generic singularities, Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 2.9), the reflection group of the billiard of 3+1-dimensional vacuum gravity near a spacelike singularity (Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai 2003 Section 8; Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 3.1), where a(n) counts the chambers reachable from the fundamental chamber after exactly n wall collisions over all initial data, so (10)-(11) give the growth rate of those outcomes (elementary reflection-group geometry, not formal content). Hypotheses are inline: the Coxeter system enters through Mathlib's CoxeterSystem with the three matrix entries as hypotheses, rho through its defining equation and 1 < rho, the Padovan sequence through its initial values and recursion; the compared statements use only core Mathlib vocabulary (CoxeterMatrix, CoxeterSystem, CoxeterSystem.length, Nat.card, PowerSeries.mk, Finset.range/Ico sums, Filter.Tendsto, Filter.atTop, nhds, real powers) — zero custom definitions. The pinned source of each Coxeter-specific imported definition, and of Nat.card and PowerSeries.mk, is quoted verbatim, with permalinks, in MATHLIB_DEFINITIONS.md (the remaining vocabulary is standard Mathlib and is not quoted), and DefinitionAudit.lean kernel-checks the facts the statements rely on (the entry 0 encodes infinity; length is the minimal word length; spheres are finite and Nat.card is their cardinality; every Coxeter matrix has a Coxeter system).

Twenty compared theorems: (1) the general identity for all p, q >= 2; (2) non-vacuity, a Coxeter matrix of that type exists for all p, q >= 2; (3)-(5) the three instances; (6) the (2,3,inf) sphere sizes a(0..4) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and the recursion a(n+5) = a(n+3) + a(n+2) for all n; (7) that the recursion fails one step earlier, a(4) != a(2) + a(1); (8) a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, for any sequence with the Padovan initial values and recursion; (9) existence and uniqueness of the plastic number; (10) the bounds; (11) the n-th-root limit; (12) monotonicity: a(n) of a (p,q,inf) system is at most a(n) of a (p',q',inf) system for p <= p', q <= q'; (13) symmetry in p and q; (14) 2 rho^n <= a(n), n >= 2, for every hyperbolic member; (15) for (p,q) != (2,2) exactly one tau > 1 solves (tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(p-1))(tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(q-1)) = 1; (16) a(n)^(1/n) -> tau; (17) tau strictly increasing in (p,q); (18) rho <= tau with equality exactly at (2,3), (3,2), so the plastic number is the minimal growth rate of the family; (19) tau < 2; (20) tau -> 2 as p, q -> infinity (for every sigma < 2 there is N with tau > sigma whenever p, q >= N). The family statements (12)-(20) give the growth rate of every hyperbolic (p, q, inf) group as the unique root tau > 1 of an explicit equation, strictly increasing in the labels, with the plastic number as the family minimum attained only at (2,3,inf) and (3,2,inf); they restrict to this family, and kernel-check there, Terragni's monotonicity (2016, Thm. A), Floyd's planar minimality (1992, p. 482) and the continuity of the growth rate (Floyd 1992; Yukita 2024). The mathematics is classical and no novelty is claimed for it: the growth series of a Coxeter group is rational and determined by its finite parabolic subgroups (Steinberg 1968; Humphreys 1990 Section 5.12); growth of planar hyperbolic Coxeter groups is Floyd 1992 and Cannon-Wagreich 1992, and the (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf) and (3,3,inf) sphere sequences are OEIS A096231, A179070 (shifted) and A054886, with generating functions derived there from Cannon-Wagreich Prop. 3.1 and, for A096231, the Padovan form a(n) = A000931(n+10) recorded; Floyd 1992 (p. 482) proves (2,3,inf) minimal among cusped planar groups and Kellerhals 2013 gives an alternative proof; Bucher-Talambutsa 2016 Prop. 18 proves statement (11) itself by a normal form and, with Mann's bound, the minimality of rho for PGL(2,Z) over all generating sets. The (p, q, inf) family is hyperbolic exactly when (p, q) differs from (2, 2); the affine (2, 2, inf) is included in (1). The contribution claimed is the kernel-checked general identity for all p, q at once, and the family statements (12)-(20) derived from it, from Mathlib's CoxeterSystem alone — Mathlib at this pin has no growth series, no exchange or deletion property and no parabolic-subgroup API — by constructing the amalgam normal forms, lifting their action to the group, proving Coxeter length equals normal-form length, and counting. No "first formalization" claim is made. Application, cited and not a claim of the entry: the (2,3,inf) group is the Weyl group of AE_3 = PGL(2,Z) (Feingold-Frenkel 1983) and, in the Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai billiard description of the Belinski-Khalatnikov-Lifshitz limit (a conjecture for generic singularities, Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 2.9), the reflection group of the billiard of 3+1-dimensional vacuum gravity near a spacelike singularity (Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai 2003 Section 8; Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 3.1), where a(n) counts the chambers reachable from the fundamental chamber after exactly n wall collisions over all initial data, so (10)-(11) give the growth rate of those outcomes (elementary reflection-group geometry, not formal content). Hypotheses are inline: the Coxeter system enters through Mathlib's CoxeterSystem with the three matrix entries as hypotheses, rho through its defining equation and 1 < rho, the Padovan sequence through its initial values and recursion; the compared statements use only core Mathlib vocabulary (CoxeterMatrix, CoxeterSystem, CoxeterSystem.length, Nat.card, PowerSeries.mk, Finset.range/Ico sums, Filter.Tendsto, Filter.atTop, nhds, real powers) — zero custom definitions. The pinned source of each Coxeter-specific imported definition, and of Nat.card and PowerSeries.mk, is quoted verbatim, with permalinks, in MATHLIB_DEFINITIONS.md (the remaining vocabulary is standard Mathlib and is not quoted), and DefinitionAudit.lean kernel-checks the facts the statements rely on (the entry 0 encodes infinity; length is the minimal word length; spheres are finite and Nat.card is their cardinality; every Coxeter matrix has a Coxeter system).

Twenty compared theorems: (1) the general identity for all p, q >= 2; (2) non-vacuity, a Coxeter matrix of that type exists for all p, q >= 2; (3)-(5) the three instances; (6) the (2,3,inf) sphere sizes a(0..4) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and the recursion a(n+5) = a(n+3) + a(n+2) for all n; (7) that the recursion fails one step earlier, a(4) != a(2) + a(1); (8) a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, for any sequence with the Padovan initial values and recursion; (9) existence and uniqueness of the plastic number; (10) the bounds; (11) the n-th-root limit; (12) monotonicity: a(n) of a (p,q,inf) system is at most a(n) of a (p',q',inf) system for p <= p', q <= q'; (13) symmetry in p and q; (14) 2 rho^n <= a(n), n >= 2, for every hyperbolic member; (15) for (p,q) != (2,2) exactly one tau > 1 solves (tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(p-1))(tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(q-1)) = 1; (16) a(n)^(1/n) -> tau; (17) tau strictly increasing in (p,q); (18) rho <= tau with equality exactly at (2,3), (3,2), so the plastic number is the minimal growth rate of the family; (19) tau < 2; (20) tau -> 2 as p, q -> infinity (for every sigma < 2 there is N with tau > sigma whenever p, q >= N). The family statements (12)-(20) give the growth rate of every hyperbolic (p, q, inf) group as the unique root tau > 1 of an explicit equation, strictly increasing in the labels, with the plastic number as the family minimum attained only at (2,3,inf) and (3,2,inf); they restrict to this family, and kernel-check there, Terragni's monotonicity (2016, Thm. A), Floyd's planar minimality (1992, p. 482) and the continuity of the growth rate (Floyd 1992; Yukita 2024). The mathematics is classical and no novelty is claimed for it: the growth series of a Coxeter group is rational and determined by its finite parabolic subgroups (Steinberg 1968; Humphreys 1990 Section 5.12); growth of planar hyperbolic Coxeter groups is Floyd 1992 and Cannon-Wagreich 1992, and the (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf) and (3,3,inf) sphere sequences are OEIS A096231, A179070 (shifted) and A054886, with generating functions derived there from Cannon-Wagreich Prop. 3.1 and, for A096231, the Padovan form a(n) = A000931(n+10) recorded; Floyd 1992 (p. 482) proves (2,3,inf) minimal among cusped planar groups and Kellerhals 2013 gives an alternative proof; Bucher-Talambutsa 2016 Prop. 18 proves statement (11) itself by a normal form and, with Mann's bound, the minimality of rho for PGL(2,Z) over all generating sets. The (p, q, inf) family is hyperbolic exactly when (p, q) differs from (2, 2); the affine (2, 2, inf) is included in (1). The contribution claimed is the kernel-checked general identity for all p, q at once, and the family statements (12)-(20) derived from it, from Mathlib's CoxeterSystem alone — Mathlib at this pin has no growth series, no exchange or deletion property and no parabolic-subgroup API — by constructing the amalgam normal forms, lifting their action to the group, proving Coxeter length equals normal-form length, and counting. No "first formalization" claim is made. Application, cited and not a claim of the entry: the (2,3,inf) group is the Weyl group of AE_3 = PGL(2,Z) (Feingold-Frenkel 1983) and, in the Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai billiard description of the Belinski-Khalatnikov-Lifshitz limit (a conjecture for generic singularities, Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 2.9), the reflection group of the billiard of 3+1-dimensional vacuum gravity near a spacelike singularity (Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai 2003 Section 8; Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 3.1), where a(n) counts the chambers reachable from the fundamental chamber after exactly n wall collisions over all initial data, so (10)-(11) give the growth rate of those outcomes (elementary reflection-group geometry, not formal content). Hypotheses are inline: the Coxeter system enters through Mathlib's CoxeterSystem with the three matrix entries as hypotheses, rho through its defining equation and 1 < rho, the Padovan sequence through its initial values and recursion; the compared statements use only core Mathlib vocabulary (CoxeterMatrix, CoxeterSystem, CoxeterSystem.length, Nat.card, PowerSeries.mk, Finset.range/Ico sums, Filter.Tendsto, Filter.atTop, nhds, real powers) — zero custom definitions. The pinned source of each Coxeter-specific imported definition, and of Nat.card and PowerSeries.mk, is quoted verbatim, with permalinks, in MATHLIB_DEFINITIONS.md (the remaining vocabulary is standard Mathlib and is not quoted), and DefinitionAudit.lean kernel-checks the facts the statements rely on (the entry 0 encodes infinity; length is the minimal word length; spheres are finite and Nat.card is their cardinality; every Coxeter matrix has a Coxeter system).

records.name: FiveGenBetti.family_spanRank_eq
records.entry_name: First Betti numbers of five-generated numerical semigroups
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization project for (F) an explicit two-parameter family of minimally five-generated numerical semigroups <m, m+1, m+k, m+2k-1, m+2k>, m = 2kq+1, whose toric ideal has spanRank exactly 4k+2. Planned scope for (W), a proposed finite-width bound beta1 <= 2w+2 (4 <= w <= 40), not all formalized: the generic fiber-graph infrastructure, both algebraic bridges (only the upper bridge is formalized; the reverse bridge is not), the corrected singleton-counting decomposition beta1 + p = 5 + N, the pair-component antichain lemma and certificate-checker soundness (not yet written). Version 1 targets F; W is stated and excluded from the release comparator. F is sorry-free at 793e759.

records.name: CountableCoordinates.finite_coordinates_of_entourage
records.entry_name: Countable-coordinate factorization for compact products
records.doc: Every continuous map from an arbitrary product of nonempty compact Hausdorff spaces into a metrizable space factors continuously through a countable subproduct. A uniform-space proof establishes countable coordinate dependence for uniformly continuous maps into separated countably generated uniform spaces. The factor for a fixed coordinate set is unique. Countably many maps share a countable coordinate set. Continuous injections into metrizable targets force only countably many nontrivial factors, giving the exact metrizability criterion for nonempty compact Hausdorff products. Empty index and empty selected-coordinate sets are allowed. These are classical results and no novelty or priority is claimed.

records.name: Submission.quadForm_two_eq_linearForm2
records.entry_name: NumericalSemigroups: Huang's quadratic form, its positivity, and its n-generator kernel windows
records.doc: Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization around the quadratic form Q(n) = sum_{i,j in G} K(g(j) - g(i)) n_i n_j of Y. Huang (arXiv:2604.13238) on the gap diagram G of the numerical semigroup <a,b>, in two parts. Part A (Huang's results, two generators): the symmetric bilinear form B of Q satisfies B(1_D, 1_E) = dinv(D, E) for subdiagrams D, E (Huang's Theorem 1.2, formalized by AxiomProver and included in `Dinv/AxiomProver.lean`); from it this work proves Q(1_D) = dinv(D) and Q(1_D) > 0 for nonempty D (Theorem 1.1), B >= 0 on the cone of nonnegative decreasing functions, and the bound Q(n) >= n_i^2 / |G| for every coordinate i (Theorem 1.3, so Q(n) >= ||n||_inf^2 / |G|), which settles Huang's positive-definiteness conjecture for Q on that cone; Theorem 1.3 had not been formalized. Part B (the author's manuscript "A Linear Algorithm for Huang's Quadratic Form on Numerical Semigroups and Density Asymptotics", Flamandzki, 2026): for generators p_1,...,p_n the generalised kernel K^(n)(d) is the inclusion-exclusion sum over sub-multisets S of the generators of (-1)^|S| times the indicator of d >= sigma(S), where sigma(S) is the sum of S; it is a step function whose jumps are the parity function pi(s) = K(s) - K(s-1). Part B states and proves: (1) for two generators a < b, Q equals the sliding-window form sum_k n_k (W+_k - W-_k); (2) for any nonempty generator list, Q(n) is a sum over the breakpoints s of K of pi(s) times the tail pair-sum T(s) = sum_{j-i >= s} n_i n_j, with at most sigma + 1 breakpoints, and the number w of active windows (intervals between consecutive breakpoints on which K is nonzero) is at most sigma, and at most 2^n - 2 for n >= 2 distinct positive generators; and (3) for strictly increasing generators p_k >= 2 with log p_n = o(n), the density w(n)/(2^n - 1) is o(P(n)) where P(n) = prod (1 - 1/p_k), equivalently delta(n)/P(n) tends to 1 for delta(n) = P(n) - w(n)/(2^n - 1). The complexity claims of the manuscript (running times of the algorithms) and its computational tables and conjectures are not formalized. The substance of Part B is the exact breakpoint decomposition of Q, the identification of the inclusion-exclusion kernel with its recursive form, and the asymptotic squeeze. Zero sorries; depends only on the three standard Lean axioms. The file `Dinv/AxiomProver.lean` is third-party code under the MIT license (see NOTICE); everything else is Apache-2.0.

records.name: PalomarDecompression.cubicCapacity
records.entry_name: Optimal Local Decompression: Uniform Finite-View Reduction
records.doc: A uniform finite-view reduction at the paper's counting-optimal k-bit vertex budget for odd maximum degree 2k-1. Given one total finite-view orientation rule with a sufficient one-bit advice guarantee, one decoder family is chosen before graph order, topology, markers, advice and payload. Every connected graph on Fin n with n>16(k+1) and degree at most 2k-1 admits an encoder recovering every edge bit at either endpoint from a 2^k-symbol vertex alphabet. The same total decoder is local across different connected graphs and arbitrary labelings, with no marker validity or encoded-input premise. Its explicit physical radius depends only on k and the oracle's radius, not n. Eight selected endpoints also cover storage capacity, advice-first coding, complete-graph counting, and bounded connected cell geometry. The external orientation algorithm, computability, general identifier assignments for the assembled theorem and mixed-component assembly remain outside the selected formal scope.

records.name: HoffmanSingleton.card_le
records.entry_name: Moore graphs of diameter two: the Hoffman–Singleton theorem
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the Hoffman–Singleton theorem on Moore graphs of diameter two. For a finite k-regular graph of diameter at most two: the Moore bound n ≤ k² + 1; if moreover the girth is at least five, then n = k² + 1 and the graph is strongly regular with parameters (k² + 1, k, 0, 1); and, if k ≥ 2, then k ∈ {2, 3, 7, 57}. Mathlib has strongly regular graphs and the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, but not this theorem.

records.name: HMP.finite_interpolation
records.entry_name: Countable-density Hewitt–Marczewski–Pondiczery theorem
records.doc: A product of at most continuum many separable topological spaces is separable. The proof constructs a countable family of finite binary tables that realizes every finite assignment of natural-number labels, then applies dense sequences in the factors. No separation, metrizability, compactness or countable-base assumption on the factors is needed. Empty factors and empty index sets are allowed. A companion theorem proves the sharp criterion for discrete Boolean cubes: Bool^I is separable exactly when the index cardinality is at most continuum. This is the classical countable-density case; no arbitrary-cardinal or algebraic generalization, novelty or priority is claimed.

records.name: HamiltonDegree.chvatal
records.entry_name: Chvátal's and Pósa's degree conditions for Hamiltonian cycles
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of two classical degree-sequence conditions for Hamiltonicity of a finite simple graph on n ≥ 3 vertices with degrees d₁ ≤ ⋯ ≤ dₙ. Chvátal's theorem (1972): if for every i < n/2, dᵢ ≤ i implies d_{n−i} ≥ n − i, then the graph is Hamiltonian (stated without sorting: if at least i vertices have degree at most i, then at least i + 1 vertices have degree at least n − i). Pósa's theorem (1962): if for every k with 1 ≤ k < (n − 1)/2 fewer than k vertices have degree at most k, and, for odd n, at most (n − 1)/2 vertices have degree at most (n − 1)/2, then the graph is Hamiltonian. Mathlib has Hamiltonian cycles but neither theorem.

records.name: RemovalLemma.card_copies_ge
records.entry_name: The graph removal lemma for every fixed graph
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the graph removal lemma of Erdős, Frankl and Rödl for an arbitrary fixed finite graph H on k vertices: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0, depending only on H and ε, such that every finite graph on n vertices with fewer than δ nᵏ labelled copies of H can be made H-free by deleting fewer than ε n² edges; equivalently (far form), a graph from which at least ε n² edges must be deleted to destroy all copies of H has at least δ nᵏ labelled copies. Also included is the counting lemma used in the proof: if parts s x (one for each vertex x of H) are robustly dense with density at least d along the edges of H, with 2kη ≤ dᵏ and #(s x) ≥ 4k/dᵏ, then at least (dᵏ/4)ᵏ ∏ #(s x) injective maps send H into G with f x ∈ s x. Mathlib has the regularity lemma and the triangle removal lemma, but not the removal lemma for a general H.

records.name: Erdos679.additive_refutation
records.entry_name: Additive strengthening of Erdos problem 679: a known refutation
records.doc: For every real additive constant C and natural cutoff K, every sufficiently large natural n admits K < k < n with omega(n-k) at least log(k)/log(log(k)) + C. Here omega counts distinct prime factors. This independently implemented proof uses a fixed primorial residue window, elementary Chebyshev estimates and Stirling bounds. It refutes the known additive strengthening and does not resolve the main multiplicative question. No mathematical novelty is claimed.

records.name: PalomarSMT.mathematical_result
records.entry_name: Tamper-proofing with self-modifying code: a Lean formalization of the threat model
records.doc: Formalizes Gregory Morse and Tamas Kozsik's paper "Tamper-Proofing with Self-Modifying Code" (arXiv:2604.12407v1). The selected statement (PalomarSMT.mathematical_result, four results T1-T4) is an abstract threat model for checksum units whose opcode state lives in the memory they checksum: a system of units with regions and code, a timeline of write, execute, check, split-view and DMA events, adversary levels L0-L4, a cost contract with lower bounds on emulation, forgery and mediation, and eight structural assumptions A1-A8 (none of the form "the attacker is detected"). An effective alarm needs a unit with a response code (at least one response byte, all of it unmodified) and either a value mismatch or a positive number k of consecutive timing failures; A6 therefore includes k > 0 and A7 includes that every unit has a response byte. The four selected results are: for every well-formed timeline of a system satisfying A1-A8, if a protected byte outside the SMC opcode bytes (which legitimately vary) is executed while the fetch view differs from the original image, an effective alarm occurs somewhere in the timeline, not necessarily before that execution (T1; executing a changed protected opcode byte is outside the goal); in a faithful split-view run every iteration with a non-zero toggle (apart from the last) is mediated, and under A3 and A5 a faithful mediated check that the cost contract admits, with such an iteration, is a timing failure (T2; not every split-view attack is claimed detected); each of the eleven assumptions is necessary, by an explicit winning adversary against a system that satisfies all the others (T3); and every well-formed timeline at level L0 or L1 with the inline timer satisfies A1, A4 and A5, while there are winning adversaries against systems satisfying every other assumption at L1 with an operating-system timer, at L2 and at L4 (T4: the removed assumption is A5 at L1 with an operating-system timer and at L2, A1 at L2, A4 at L4). Proved in the same development but NOT part of this record (they are not in the Comparator configuration): the paper's Harvard/von Neumann observation (C01, C02), a general fact about observation-preserving simulation whose time bound assumes the per-read charge it uses; the three-quadword forgery of the checksum and the proof that two quadwords do not suffice (the selected T3 witness for A8 is a single two-quadword collision pair); the x86-64 model of the kernels, the static kernel against its C emulation, the 296-unit unrolled kernel at an abstract level and at the instruction level, the byte layout against assembler output, a clear-count contract checked against the paper's tables, timers, the noise estimator, the detection predicate and the data ratios, and native test vectors for the corrected sources.

records.name: TutteFactor.tutte_f_factor
records.entry_name: Tutte's f-factor theorem
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Tutte's f-factor theorem: a finite simple graph G has a spanning subgraph H with deg_H v = f v for every vertex v if and only if, for all disjoint vertex sets S and T, q(S, T) ≤ ∑_{v ∈ S} f v − ∑_{v ∈ T} f v + ∑_{v ∈ T} deg_{G−S} v, where q(S, T) is the number of connected components C of G − (S ∪ T) for which ∑_{v ∈ C} f v + e(C, T) is odd and deg_{G−S} v is the number of neighbours of v outside S. Mathlib has Tutte's 1-factor theorem but not the f-factor theorem.

records.name: ChordalClasses.minimalSeparator_isClique
records.entry_name: Chordal, split, threshold and cograph structure
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of classical structure theorems for finite simple graphs. Chordal graphs: every minimal a–b separator is a clique, a nonempty finite chordal graph has a simplicial vertex, and a connected non-complete one has two non-adjacent simplicial vertices (Dirac 1961); a finite graph is chordal iff it has a perfect elimination order (Fulkerson–Gross 1965), iff it is the intersection graph of subtrees of a finite tree (Gavril 1974); a nonempty finite chordal graph has treewidth ω − 1, and every finite graph has ω ≤ tw + 1. Split graphs: split iff the graph and its complement are chordal, iff no induced 2K₂, C₄ or C₅ (Földes–Hammer 1977). Threshold graphs: threshold iff no induced 2K₂, C₄ or P₄ (Chvátal–Hammer 1977), iff split and a cograph (no induced P₄). Mathlib has none of these graph classes; their definitions are stated in the Challenge.

Split graphs: split iff the graph and its complement are chordal, iff no induced 2K₂, C₄ or C₅ (Földes–Hammer 1977). Threshold graphs: threshold iff no induced 2K₂, C₄ or P₄ (Chvátal–Hammer 1977), iff split and a cograph (no induced P₄). Mathlib has none of these graph classes; their definitions are stated in the Challenge.

records.name: Erdos684.upper_bound
records.entry_name: Elementary bounds for Erdos problem 684
records.doc: Let U(n,k) be the full prime-power part of the binomial coefficient n choose k supported on primes at most k. For all sufficiently large n, there exists k at most n with k at most 514(log n)^2 and U(n,k) greater than n squared. For arbitrarily large n greater than one, U(n,k) equals one throughout k at most (log n)/8. This independent Mathlib-only implementation adapts the known residue averaging and prime-power obstruction of APSSV26 with coarse Chebyshev constants. It does not formalize that paper's sharper coefficients or Bae's stronger registered lower bound. The optimal order remains open and no mathematical novelty is claimed.

records.name: BucklingChallenge.area_inequality
records.entry_name: Planar Pólya–Szegő Buckling Inequality
records.doc: Lean formalization proving the planar Polya-Szego conjecture for the first buckling eigenvalue. For open planar sets of positive finite area, it proves the sharp area inequality and characterizes equality by exact equality with an open disk. It retains the original Sobolev-space, variational eigenvalue and Bessel definitions, and includes the disk eigenvalue and buckling–Dirichlet comparison.

records.name: JaegerFlow.exists_even_cover_of_trees
records.entry_name: Jaeger's 4-flow theorem
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Jaeger's 4-flow theorem: every finite 4-edge-connected simple graph has a nowhere-zero integer 4-flow, i.e. an antisymmetric function on darts with values in {±1, ±2, ±3} that is conserved at every vertex. Also proved: a graph with two edge-disjoint spanning trees has its edges covered by two even subgraphs (a nowhere-zero ℤ₂ × ℤ₂-flow) and has a nowhere-zero integer 4-flow. Mathlib has no flows. Jaeger's 8-flow theorem for bridgeless graphs is not included.

records.name: NormalizerLean.Gamma0R_le_normG_GammaDeltaR
records.entry_name: Normalizers of Γ_Δ(N), Γ(N) and ±Γ₁(N)
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of the groups Γ_Δ(N) between Γ₁(N) and Γ₀(N), and the quotients Nor(Γ)/Γ, the modular automorphism groups of the curves X_Δ(N): a generalization of Newman's description of the normalizer to Γ_Δ(N); Nor(Γ(N)) = SL₂(ℤ), so the modular automorphism group of X(N) is SL₂(ℤ/N)/{±1}; and, for N ≠ 4, Nor(±Γ₁(N)) is generated by Γ₀(N) and the Atkin–Lehner elements, so X₁(N) has 2^ω(N) φ(N)/2 modular automorphisms for N ≥ 3 (N = 4 is an exception). 34 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of the groups Γ_Δ(N) between Γ₁(N) and Γ₀(N), and the quotients Nor(Γ)/Γ, the modular automorphism groups of the curves X_Δ(N): a generalization of Newman's description of the normalizer to Γ_Δ(N); Nor(Γ(N)) = SL₂(ℤ), so the modular automorphism group of X(N) is SL₂(ℤ/N)/{±1}; and, for N ≠ 4, Nor(±Γ₁(N)) is generated by Γ₀(N) and the Atkin–Lehner elements, so X₁(N) has 2^ω(N) φ(N)/2 modular automorphisms for N ≥ 3 (N = 4 is an exception). 34 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: CommonCycle.exists_cycle_through
records.entry_name: Dirac's theorem: k vertices of a k-connected graph lie on a common cycle
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of Dirac's 1960 theorem: in a k-connected finite simple graph with k ≥ 2 (more than k vertices, and connected after deleting any set of fewer than k vertices), any set of at most k vertices lies on a common cycle. In particular, in a 2-connected finite graph any two vertices lie on a common cycle. Cycles are Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle`. Mathlib does not have this theorem.

records.name: NormalizerLean.hPart_isGreatest
records.entry_name: The normalizer of Γ₀(N): Newman's theorem, and the order and presentations of B(N)
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about B(N) = Nor(Γ₀(N))/Γ₀(N), the normalizer of Γ₀(N) in SL₂(ℝ) modulo Γ₀(N), for every N ≥ 1: Newman's theorem describing the normalizer, in both directions; the order |B(N)| = 2^ω(n) ψ(N)/ψ(n), where h is the largest divisor of 24 with h² ∣ N and n = N/h²; generators and complete presentations of B(N) for every N; a criterion for B(N) to be the internal direct product of its local factors; B(18) ≅ S₄; and the errors in the published presentations: the Akbaş–Singerman relation fails in B(256), and Bars's presentations at levels 32, 64 and 128 define infinite groups, while completed presentations present B(32) and B(64) and Bars's presentation at level 256 presents B(256). 36 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about B(N) = Nor(Γ₀(N))/Γ₀(N), the normalizer of Γ₀(N) in SL₂(ℝ) modulo Γ₀(N), for every N ≥ 1: Newman's theorem describing the normalizer, in both directions; the order |B(N)| = 2^ω(n) ψ(N)/ψ(n), where h is the largest divisor of 24 with h² ∣ N and n = N/h²; generators and complete presentations of B(N) for every N; a criterion for B(N) to be the internal direct product of its local factors; B(18) ≅ S₄; and the errors in the published presentations: the Akbaş–Singerman relation fails in B(256), and Bars's presentations at levels 32, 64 and 128 define infinite groups, while completed presentations present B(32) and B(64) and Bars's presentation at level 256 presents B(256). 36 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: NormalizerLean.normG_level_form
records.entry_name: Modular automorphisms of Cartan modular curves of prime level
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of the groups defining the split and non-split Cartan modular curves and their normalizer curves: for any level N, every element of the normalizer of a group containing Γ(N) is a rational matrix of a restricted form; X_sp(N) ≅ X₀(N²); X_sp(p) (p ≥ 5) and X_ns(p) (p odd) have exactly 2 modular automorphisms; X_sp⁺(p) (p ≥ 7) and X_ns⁺(p) (p ≥ 5) have none, and both bounds on p are sharp. 17 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of the groups defining the split and non-split Cartan modular curves and their normalizer curves: for any level N, every element of the normalizer of a group containing Γ(N) is a rational matrix of a restricted form; X_sp(N) ≅ X₀(N²); X_sp(p) (p ≥ 5) and X_ns(p) (p odd) have exactly 2 modular automorphisms; X_sp⁺(p) (p ≥ 7) and X_ns⁺(p) (p ≥ 5) have none, and both bounds on p are sharp. 17 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: SigmaFrechet.exists_sequence
records.entry_name: Fréchet–Urysohn Σ-products of first-countable spaces
records.doc: The countable-support Sigma-product of arbitrary first-countable topological factors, relative to an explicit basepoint and with the ordinary product-induced topology, is Frechet-Urysohn. An adaptive finite-coordinate schedule constructs a sequence from each set converging to any of its closure points. The index set may be arbitrary, including empty, and no separation assumption is used for this theorem. Companions give countable tightness and subspace inheritance, density in the full product, T1 countable-closure support control and sequential closedness, and nonsequentiality of an uncountable discrete Boolean cube. No normality, W-space, arbitrary Frechet-factor, compactness or novel-mathematics result is asserted.

records.name: DeltaIntro.DeltaTheoremA
records.entry_name: The local dynamical structure of Δ* sets via a new Furstenberg family algebra
records.doc:
This development formalizes in Lean 4 the results of the paper "The local dynamical structure of Δ* sets via a new Furstenberg family algebra", which strengthens the connection between the combinatorics of difference sets and the dynamics of group rotations.
Let S be a discrete semigroup. A set A ⊆ S is syndetic if there is a finite F ⊆ S with S = ∪_{f ∈ F} f⁻¹A; a Δ set if there is a sequence s₁, s₂, … in S with s_j ∈ s_i A for all i < j; and a Bohr_0 set if it contains the preimage of an open neighborhood of the identity under a semigroup homomorphism from S to a finite-dimensional torus. Dually, a set is thick, a Δ* set, or a set of Bohr recurrence according as it meets every syndetic, every Δ, or every Bohr_0 subset of S. Bohr_0 sets in the integers are the almost periodic sets of classical interest, and Δ* sets are combinatorially large, being syndetic and rich in additive patterns.
The definition of a Δ set used here is the one given for general semigroups by Hindman, who calls these rQ sets, Q for quotient; in a commutative semigroup his left- and right-handed variants agree. It does not require the witnessing sequence to be injective, and so is slightly more inclusive than the classical difference-set definition. In the positive integers the two agree exactly: if A consists of positive integers and s_j − s_i ∈ A for all i < j then the sequence is strictly increasing, so A contains the difference set (S − S) ∩ ℕ of the infinite set S = {s₁, s₂, …}, and conversely. The two notions separate only in a semigroup containing an element a with sa = s for some s, where the constant sequence makes every set containing such an a a Δ set. In the integers the element 0 is of this kind, so a Δ set in the present sense is either a classical difference set or a set containing 0, and a Δ* set is exactly a classical Δ* set that contains 0.
The main result (Theorem A) is that Δ* sets in an arbitrary commutative semigroup carry local Bohr structure: if A ⊆ S is a Δ* set, then for every thick H ⊆ S there is a thick H′ ⊆ H and a Bohr_0 set B with A ∩ H′ = B ∩ H′. This generalizes results of Bergelson, Furstenberg and Weiss and of Host and Kra from the positive integers to arbitrary commutative semigroups by a purely topological-dynamical route in place of the ergodic- theoretic arguments used in the integer case. Theorem B is the dual formulation, in terms of Δ sets and sets of Bohr recurrence, that the proof actually establishes: if A ⊆ S admits a thick H such that A ∩ H′ is a set of Bohr recurrence for every thick H′ ⊆ H, then A is a Δ set. Theorem C exhibits a second instance of local structure by the same method: in a countable commutative semigroup, every C* set agrees with an IP* set on a thick subset of any prescribed thick set.  Theorem C also formulates the equivalent dual statement, just as Theorem B is in relation to Theorem A.
Theorem D supplies the algebraic framework the arguments rest on. A Furstenberg family on a set S is an upward-closed collection of subsets of S. On the Furstenberg families of a non-empty set, two binary operations, family meet and family join, are described and shown to be associative, commutative and monotone. Together with the family dual, they satisfy De Morgan-type laws. Family join has appeared before in the literature; family meet, as presented here, is believed to be new. The algebra reduces the equivalence of Theorems A and B to a short computation and makes similar reformulations in Ramsey theory routine.
The proofs of Theorems A and B depend on a companion result, formalized here but the subject of another Palomar entry, that the regionally proximal relation is an equivalence relation for minimal actions of commutative semigroups. The development runs to roughly 20,000 lines of Lean across 17 files and formalizes every lemma, proposition, corollary and theorem of the paper; the registered statements are Theorems A, B, C and D. Proved along the way, and not available in Mathlib, is the classical fact that the characters of a compact abelian group separate its points.

Dually, a set is thick, a Δ* set, or a set of Bohr recurrence according as it meets every syndetic, every Δ, or every Bohr_0 subset of S. Bohr_0 sets in the integers are the almost periodic sets of classical interest, and Δ* sets are combinatorially large, being syndetic and rich in additive patterns.
The definition of a Δ set used here is the one given for general semigroups by Hindman, who calls these rQ sets, Q for quotient; in a commutative semigroup his left- and right-handed variants agree. It does not require the witnessing sequence to be injective, and so is slightly more inclusive than the classical difference-set definition. In the positive integers the two agree exactly: if A consists of positive integers and s_j − s_i ∈ A for all i < j then the sequence is strictly increasing, so A contains the difference set (S − S) ∩ ℕ of the infinite set S = {s₁, s₂, …}, and conversely. The two notions separate only in a semigroup containing an element a with sa = s for some s, where the constant sequence makes every set containing such an a a Δ set. In the integers the element 0 is of this kind, so a Δ set in the present sense is either a classical difference set or a set containing 0, and a Δ* set is exactly a classical Δ* set that contains 0.
The main result (Theorem A) is that Δ* sets in an arbitrary commutative semigroup carry local Bohr structure: if A ⊆ S is a Δ* set, then for every thick H ⊆ S there is a thick H′ ⊆ H and a Bohr_0 set B with A ∩ H′ = B ∩ H′. This generalizes results of Bergelson, Furstenberg and Weiss and of Host and Kra from the positive integers to arbitrary commutative semigroups by a purely topological-dynamical route in place of the ergodic- theoretic arguments used in the integer case. Theorem B is the dual formulation, in terms of Δ sets and sets of Bohr recurrence, that the proof actually establishes: if A ⊆ S admits a thick H such that A ∩ H′ is a set of Bohr recurrence for every thick H′ ⊆ H, then A is a Δ set. Theorem C exhibits a second instance of local structure by the same method: in a countable commutative semigroup, every C* set agrees with an IP* set on a thick subset of any prescribed thick set.  Theorem C also formulates the equivalent dual statement, just as Theorem B is in relation to Theorem A.
Theorem D supplies the algebraic framework the arguments rest on. A Furstenberg family on a set S is an upward-closed collection of subsets of S. On the Furstenberg families of a non-empty set, two binary operations, family meet and family join, are described and shown to be associative, commutative and monotone. Together with the family dual, they satisfy De Morgan-type laws. Family join has appeared before in the literature; family meet, as presented here, is believed to be new. The algebra reduces the equivalence of Theorems A and B to a short computation and makes similar reformulations in Ramsey theory routine.
The proofs of Theorems A and B depend on a companion result, formalized here but the subject of another Palomar entry, that the regionally proximal relation is an equivalence relation for minimal actions of commutative semigroups. The development runs to roughly 20,000 lines of Lean across 17 files and formalizes every lemma, proposition, corollary and theorem of the paper; the registered statements are Theorems A, B, C and D. Proved along the way, and not available in Mathlib, is the classical fact that the characters of a compact abelian group separate its points.

records.name: AdjacencySpectrum.average_degree_le
records.entry_name: Spectral bounds on the chromatic and independence numbers
records.doc: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of classical eigenvalue bounds for a finite simple graph G on a nonempty vertex type, with λ_max and λ_min the largest and smallest eigenvalues of its real adjacency matrix: the average degree is at most λ_max and λ_max is at most the maximum degree (Collatz–Sinogowitz); G is (⌊λ_max⌋ + 1)-colourable (Wilf 1967); if G has an edge, every proper colouring uses at least 1 − λ_max/λ_min colours (Hoffman 1970); and if G is k-regular with k ≥ 1, every independent set has at most n(−λ_min)/(k − λ_min) vertices (Hoffman's ratio bound). Mathlib has the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices but none of these bounds.

records.name: NormalizerLean.GammaH_map
records.entry_name: Normalizers of the congruence subgroups Γ_H
records.doc: Formal statements and proofs, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, about the normalizers in SL₂(ℝ) of every congruence subgroup Γ ⊇ Γ(N), that is, of every Γ_H for H ≤ SL₂(ℤ/N): Nor(Γ)/Γ is finite, of order at most [SL₂(ℤ) : Γ]·Σ_{D ∣ N} ψ(D); the local restrictions of Dose–Lido–Mercuri on the determinants of normalizing matrices; if, at every p ∣ N, H mod p fixes no line or H mod p^{v_p(N)} lies in a split Cartan subgroup, then Nor(Γ_H)/Γ_H ≅ N(H)/H; and at prime level the order is always [N(H) : H], or 2·[N(H) : H] when H fixes exactly one line. 21 theorems, no sorry, only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

records.name: Erdos685Research.tendsto_omega_centralBinom
records.entry_name: Distinct prime divisors of central binomial coefficients
records.doc: A formal proof of the classical asymptotic omega(binomial(2n,n)) times log n divided by n tending to log 4. The proof combines prime-power estimates, central-binomial bounds, a prime-factor cutoff, and elementary logarithmic limits; it does not use the prime number theorem. This strengthens the earlier finite lower-bound package to a full asymptotic theorem. It does not solve the uniform conjecture in Erdos problem 685 and claims no new mathematical theorem.

records.name: ArithmeticOfTime.padovan_minimal_unique
records.entry_name: The Arithmetic of Time: the slowest settling clock on at most three letters is the Padovan substitution, unique up to mirror image, and both minimal rules are chiral
records.doc: Five compared theorems. Among all substitutions on at most three letters whose incidence matrix has a Pisot eigenvalue θ > 1, the least such θ is the plastic number ρ, the real root of x³ = x + 1, attained only by the Padovan rule a ↦ b, b ↦ c, c ↦ ab and its mirror c ↦ ba, up to renaming the letters; both minimal rules are chiral, in opposite directions. Precisely: (1) for a substitution σ on k ≤ 3 letters (images may be empty) and a real eigenvalue θ > 1 of its integer incidence matrix that is a Pisot number, ρ ≤ θ, and θ = ρ exactly when, after renaming the letters, σ is the Padovan rule or its mirror; no primitivity or unit hypothesis; (2) the same classification for every real eigenvalue, with no Pisot hypothesis; (3) a 3 × 3 natural matrix with characteristic polynomial x³ − x − 1 is the Padovan matrix after one simultaneous permutation of rows and columns; (4) Siegel's bound ρ ≤ θ for Pisot numbers of degree at most three (Siegel 1944, restricted; not new; proved through the minimal Mahler measures of registered entry PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004); (5) under the Padovan rule the word ca is a factor of the fifth iterate from the seed a, and ac is a factor of no iterate from any seed; under its mirror, the reverse. The uniqueness was stated without proof by Mercat (2020) for substitutions on three letters; the contribution is a kernel-checked proof of the combined statement, for every real eigenvalue and with no primitivity, unit or non-erasing hypothesis (in the equality case these are consequences: θ = ρ forces k = 3 and characteristic polynomial x³ − x − 1), together with the chirality of both minimal rules. No first-formalization claim is made. That ρ itself is a Pisot eigenvalue of the Padovan matrix, so that the bound is attained, is proved in Supplement.lean and not compared. Companion of registered entry PALOMAR-2026-08-19-000006.

records.name: OAI.EuclideanRamsey.Radian.radian_configuration
records.entry_name: The radian nine-gon is Euclidean Ramsey iff e^(i theta) is algebraic
records.doc: Theorem D: for real theta, the nine points (cos k theta, sin k theta), k = 0, ..., 8, of the Euclidean plane are distinct, lie on the unit circle and are not Euclidean Ramsey when tan(theta/2) is transcendental; and whenever they are distinct, they are Ramsey if and only if cos theta and sin theta are algebraic (that is, iff e^(i theta) is algebraic), if and only if tan(theta/2) is algebraic. This is an iff for a whole one-parameter family, where earlier explicit examples with a transcendental parameter (OpenAI's Proposition 7.7 and Corollary 7.5) settle single sets: the same nine-point pattern is Ramsey or not exactly as e^(i theta) is algebraic or transcendental. Nine is the exact threshold (eight consecutive multiples are Ramsey for every theta; by hand, in spherical-ramsey), and at theta = e the question becomes whether e^(i e) is algebraic, which appears to be open. Ramsey is OpenAI's definition from result 172 (for every r >= 2 there is D such that every r-colouring of R^D contains a monochromatic congruent copy). The statements are given in OpenAI's vocabulary plus the two-line definition of the nine points, and again with no definitions beyond Mathlib. The non-Ramsey direction mirrors OpenAI's nine-point proof (their Proposition 7.6): the coordinate field is Q(tan(theta/2)), its tensor square embeds in Q(T, U), and the denominator-cleared 9x9 evaluation matrix is nonsingular, certified at (T, U) = (2, 3) by an explicit integer triangular factorization checked by decide +kernel; OpenAI's linear obstruction concludes. The converse uses the theorem that finite spherical sets with algebraic coordinates are Ramsey (prior work of JD-Jones-ASES, Rogerhu12 and atimics; proved again here in Lean on OpenAI's development). The proof builds on OpenAI's complete Lean proof of the classification (openai/math fd4aeeb2), whose 35 files used here are included with header-only changes for the Lean module system. This repository is a module-system port, with no statement or proof line changed apart from a namespace rename, of Lean already public as rope AV3 of spherical-ramsey v1.1.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23396387), packaged so that Theorem D can be checked on its own. All theorems depend on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only.
